transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you—what brings you in today, and what would you like help with?

I’ve been having a lot of trouble actually following through on things, especially with school projects and some freelance work I’m doing. I get really excited at the beginning, but I end up finishing late or only getting things done when there’s some kind of last‑minute crisis, and it’s starting to mess with my grades and work, so I want to figure out what’s going on.

When things don’t go as planned—like with school or work—do you mainly feel anxious or sad about it, or do you also notice intense, rapidly shifting emotions and big reactions that often cause problems in your relationships with others?

It’s mostly this steady mix of anxiety and feeling disappointed in myself, like I’ve let people down or I’m going to screw up my future. I don’t usually have huge mood swings, but I have sent a couple of panicky emails or gotten snappy in group chats when I’m stressed, and then felt bad about it afterward.

When you sit down to work, do you find your mind frequently drifting off and getting distracted by unrelated thoughts or stimuli, or is it more that you stay focused on the task but are stuck worrying and overthinking about how it might go wrong?

It’s definitely more that my mind drifts off and gets distracted by random stuff or whatever’s around me. I’ll be watching a lecture or coding and suddenly realize I’ve been staring at the screen while thinking about my plants or a Slack message, and then I have to rewind or refocus over and over.

Have you had this kind of distractibility and trouble finishing things since you were a child in school, in more than one setting (like both at home and at school), or is it something that only started in the last few years during college and work?

It’s been a thing since I was a kid, both at school and at home. Teachers used to write comments like “bright but daydreams and rushes,” and I’d forget to turn in homework I’d actually done and get in trouble for blurting out answers and fidgeting, but it’s gotten way more unmanageable in the last year or so with harder classes and freelance stuff.

Outside of situations where there’s a clear deadline or task you’re behind on, do you often find yourself worrying excessively about many different things most days for at least six months, or is the anxiety mainly tied to your school and work performance problems?

It’s mainly tied to school and work stuff—deadlines, big projects, and realizing I’ve misjudged how long things will take. I don’t feel like I’m constantly worrying about everything all the time; it spikes when I’m behind or think I might tank a class or lose a client and mess up future opportunities.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were [F90.0, F41.1]. The patient describes lifelong patterns of distractibility, daydreaming, fidgeting, blurting out answers, and chronic difficulty completing tasks across multiple settings (school and home), now causing significant impairment in college and freelance work. This trajectory strongly supports a neurodevelopmental attention-related condition. The anxiety the patient reports is situational and clearly tied to academic and work performance, rather than being excessive, generalized, and present on most days for at least six months across many domains of life, which makes a primary generalized anxiety condition much less likely. Therefore, F41.1 is removed from the differential, and F90.0 remains as the current candidate. Further questioning about other symptom domains, impairment, and rule-outs is still needed, so this is not yet final.

inference_history.note: Initial presentation includes difficulty with task follow-through, procrastination, and reliance on last-minute pressure, which raises concern for an attention/organizational disorder, an anxiety-related issue, or a mood/personality factor. At this very early stage, there are no previous candidates to compare against, so this is a broad initial differential. F90.0 (a neurodevelopmental condition with inattention/organization problems) is considered because of chronic-sounding problems with sustaining effort and completing tasks. F41.1 (an anxiety-related condition) is included because avoidance and procrastination can be driven by worry, perfectionism, or fear of failure. F32.0 (a mild mood episode) is included because low motivation, impaired concentration, and reduced initiative can present as difficulty following through on tasks, though no clear mood symptoms have been described yet. F60.3 (a personality-related condition involving instability and impulsivity) is included more tentatively, as difficulty with consistency and follow-through can sometimes be part of broader interpersonal and self-regulation problems; there is no direct evidence yet, but it remains on the very broad initial list. Further questioning is needed about attention, hyperactivity/impulsivity, anxiety, mood, duration, developmental history, and interpersonal patterns to refine the differential.

inference_history.note: Previously the candidates were [F90.0, F41.1, F32.0]. The patient reports lifelong symptoms beginning in childhood, across settings, with clear patterns of inattention (daydreaming, forgetting to turn in homework, needing to rewind lectures) and some hyperactive/impulsive features (blurting out answers, fidgeting). These symptoms are now causing significant impairment with more demanding tasks, which is consistent with the first candidate. Anxiety is present but appears secondary—mainly as worry and self‑criticism in response to performance problems and deadlines—so the second candidate remains possible as a comorbid or contributing condition. There is no description of persistent low mood, anhedonia, or other core depressive symptoms; the sadness described is situational and tied to performance, so the third candidate (a depressive episode) is now less likely and has been removed. Further questioning is still needed to clarify the full symptom profile, degree of functional impairment, and the nature and severity of the anxiety, so the list is not final.

opening_question.question: Hello, it’s good to meet you—what brings you in today, and what would you like help with?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports a longstanding pattern, beginning in childhood and present across home and school, of distractibility, daydreaming, fidgeting, blurting out answers, and difficulty completing tasks unless under last‑minute pressure. These symptoms have become more impairing with increasing academic and work demands and are causing significant functional impairment in school and freelance work. Anxiety is present but appears secondary to performance problems rather than a pervasive, free‑floating worry pattern, making ADHD, predominantly inattentive type, the primary diagnosis.
